title: Like grain, mortals ripen and come again
theme: The boy urges his father to keep his word: those before and those now were true to theirs, and life is too short for a lie.

words.meaning: look back upon, consider in order

words.context: Śaṅkara: «वर्तमानाश्च अपरे साधवो» — the good who live now; the letters also allow pare, ‘the later ones’

sandhi.rule: tathā + apare → tathāpare, ā + a → ā, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः); the base prints a space, so the letters can also be read tathā pare.

sandhi.type: final m before a vowel; savarṇa-dīrgha
sandhi.rule: m stays before a vowel; iva + ājāyate → ivājāyate, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः).

morphology.note: Passive of pac, ‘cook, ripen’: a mortal ‘is ripened’ — grows old and dies — like grain.
ā + jan, ‘comes to be again’. Madhva’s text reads sasyam iva jāyate punaḥ, without ā (corrections.json).

translation.literal: Consider how [were] those before; observe how [are] the others. Like grain a mortal ripens; like grain he is born again.
translation.readable: ‘Think how our forebears acted, and see how good people act now. A mortal ripens like grain, and like grain he springs up again.’

anvaya: पूर्वे यथा [वृत्ताः], [तत्] अनुपश्य । अपरे तथा [वर्तन्ते], [तत्] प्रतिपश्य । मर्त्यः सस्यम् इव पच्यते, सस्यम् इव पुनः आजायते ॥
syntax: Two imperatives (‘consider’, ‘observe’) with clauses of manner whose verbs are understood, then two comparisons with sasyam iva, ‘like grain’. The verse is the boy’s argument to his father.

ambiguities.note: The base prints तथा परे; the letters can be tathā pare (‘so the later ones’) or tathā apare (‘so the others’). Śaṅkara and Raṅgarāmānuja both comment apare, ‘the good who live now’.

ambiguities.topic: Who speaks, and to what end?
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara and Raṅgarāmānuja: the boy speaks to his repentant father, urging him to keep his word and send him to Death. The point of the grain image is that life is brief, so a lie gains nothing.

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: Anuṣṭubh with a hypermetric second line: 16 + 18 syllables as written (each pāda of the second line has nine).

beginner: The father seems to regret his angry words. The boy answers him: think how our ancestors lived, and look at how good people live now. None of them made their word false. And why would anyone break their word? Life is short. A human being ripens and falls like grain, and like grain springs up again in another life. Nothing lasting is won by a lie in so brief a span. So keep your word, father: send me to Death. It is a remarkable speech for a child. He is not holding his father to a technicality; he is reminding him that truthfulness is what holds a life together when everything else passes.
analogy: Like a harvest field: the grain ripens, is cut, and the field grows again next season — no single stalk lasts long enough to be worth a lie.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: Consider those before and observe those now; a mortal ripens like grain and comes up again like grain.

commentary.q: What is the boy asking of his father?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: to keep his word. The ancestors and the good never made their word false — and no one becomes free of age and death by a lie: «न च मृषाभूतं कृत्वा कश्चिदजरामरो भवति». So: «पालयात्मनः सत्यम्», keep your own truth, and send me to Yama. Raṅgarāmānuja: «एवमनित्ये जीवलोके किं मृषाकरणेन», in so impermanent a world, what is gained by falsehood? — «प्रेषय मां मृत्यवे».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: Śaṅkara reads apare, the good of the present: «वर्तमानाश्च अपरे साधवो यथा वर्तन्ते». The printed spacing (तथा परे) would allow pare, ‘the later ones’; the commentators’ reading needs the a.

advaita.text: An argument for truthfulness from impermanence: «न च मृषाभूतं कृत्वा कश्चिदजरामरो भवति» … «पालयात्मनः सत्यम्».

visistadvaita.text: The same argument: «एवमनित्ये जीवलोके किं मृषाकरणेन» — keep the truth and send me to Death.

schools.disagreement: None of substance; Madhva’s bhāṣya has no separate comment on this mantra.

parallels.quote: जातस्य हि ध्रुवो मृत्युर्ध्रुवं जन्म मृतस्य च
parallels.note: The Gītā’s ‘for the born, death is certain, and birth for the dead’ states plainly the cycle that the grain image pictures.

contemporary.text: A promise made rashly is still a promise. The boy asks his father to act as people of integrity have always acted, even when it costs him dearly. This is a modern reflection, not the text’s claim.

reflect.beginner: Is it ever right to keep a promise you regret making?
reflect.deeper: How does the shortness of life bear on whether a lie is worth telling?
reflect.practice: Keep one small promise today that you would rather not keep, and notice what it costs and what it gives.

flags.note: Madhva’s text reads sasyam iva jāyate punaḥ for sasyam ivājāyate punaḥ (corrections.json).
